narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest influences, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile (1st) after your first year and only the second decile after your third year. These standings are well below the average performance of students who were accepted, signaling that your academic record in law school was significantly weaker than most successful applicants.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the third most important factor. This score actually worked in your favor by slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure, yet it was not enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic performance in law school made success on the bar exam uncertain enough that the admissions committee could not offer you a place.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Retake the LSAT if possible, aim for a noticeably higher score, and consider additional bar-preparation coursework or a structured study program that directly addresses the gaps shown in your early law-school performance. With clearer evidence of improvement in those key areas, a future application would be viewed much more favorably. (248 words)
